query.original_query: interpretable features steering generative models physical fields PDE boundary conditions dimensional consistency

sub_queries.semantic_query: interpretable features steering generative models neural networks controlling physical fields PDE boundary conditions dimensional consistency mechanistic interpretability
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the extent to which interpretable features learned by sparse autoencoders in generative models can be leveraged to control physical fields governed by partial differential equations. Our analysis focuses on a neural network trained to solve boundary value problems, where we apply dictionary learning to the residual stream of the model. We find that individual monosemantic features correspond to specific physical modes, such as sinusoidal basis functions or localized boundary effects, and that these features exhibit dimensional consistency with the underlying PDE parameters. By performing feature steering—selectively activating or suppressing these sparse features—we demonstrate targeted manipulation of the predicted field, including adjustments to boundary condition amplitude and spatial frequency. Results show that steering a single feature can produce physically meaningful changes in the output while preserving the solution’s adherence to the PDE. Our analysis reveals that the model’s internal representations encode a decomposition of the solution space into interpretable, physically grounded components, enabling direct control over the generative process without retraining.

sub_queries.semantic_query: physics-informed neural networks PDE boundary conditions dimensional consistency interpretable features steering physical fields generative models
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the role of dimensional consistency as an inductive bias in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with complex boundary conditions. By embedding interpretable, physically scaled features derived from the governing equations into the network architecture, we examine how dimensional homogeneity constraints affect the steering of latent physical fields during training. The study systematically evaluates the impact of boundary condition encoding strategies—hard versus soft constraints—on the convergence and accuracy of the predicted field solutions. Results indicate that enforcing dimensional consistency through feature normalization significantly improves the network’s ability to generalize to unseen boundary configurations, particularly in advection-dominated and elliptic regimes. Findings support the hypothesis that interpretable feature engineering, grounded in the dimensional analysis of the PDE system, enhances the generative capacity of PINNs by reducing the solution manifold’s sensitivity to loss weighting. This work provides empirical evidence that domain-informed architectural choices are critical for robust field reconstruction in computational physics.

papers.title: TIME: A Transparent, Interpretable, Model-Adaptive and Explainable Neural Network for Dynamic Physical Processes
papers.research_question: Can we recover an invariant structure (PDE) from dense space-time observations, detect anomalies, and make the network interpretable and transparent?
papers.core_contribution: A low-weight, fully convolutional encoder-decoder network that learns interpretable representations of PDEs from space-time data, with transparency and explainability.
papers.conclusion: The TIME network is effective for learning PDE representations and provides interpretability and explainability, allowing modelers to verify the network's workings against their domain knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The network can learn PDE kernels that approximate differential operators.
Network design (depth and number of kernels) affects interpretability and accuracy.
The network is robust to scaling and can detect missing data as anomalies in activation maps.
A compact representation (appropriate depth and kernel count) performs best while maintaining interpretability.
High-weight representations are redundant and impact interpretability.
future_direction: Imbibe complicated processes with additional domain constraints.
papers.abstract: Partial Differential Equations are infinite dimensional encoded representations of physical processes. However, imbibing multiple observation data towards a coupled representation presents significant challenges. We present a fully convolutional architecture that captures the invariant structure of the domain to reconstruct the observable system. The proposed architecture is significantly low-weight compared to other networks for such problems. Our intent is to learn coupled dynamic processes interpreted as deviations from true kernels representing isolated processes for model-adaptivity. Experimental analysis shows that our architecture is robust and transparent in capturing process kernels and system anomalies. We also show that high weights representation is not only redundant but also impacts network interpretability. Our design is guided by domain knowledge, with isolated process representations serving as ground truths for verification. These allow us to identify redundant kernels and their manifestations in activation maps to guide better designs that are both interpretable and explainable unlike traditional deep-nets.

papers.title: Randomness and signal propagation in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): A neural PDE perspective
papers.research_question: What are the implications of the random-like weight matrices in trained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for signal propagation and stability, and how can they be understood through the lens of neural PDEs and random matrix theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that trained PINN weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with random matrix theory, and that signal propagation in such networks can be interpreted through neural PDEs, with stability governed by the numerical properties of the underlying discretization schemes.
papers.conclusion: The neural PDE framework provides a useful perspective for interpreting signal propagation in deep networks, and the stability properties of the underlying numerical schemes are reflected in the structure of the learned weight matrices.
papers.key_findings:
Trained PINN weight matrices exhibit statistical and spectral properties consistent with predictions from random matrix theory, preferring a high-entropy regime.
Random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs.
The numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network.
Explicit numerical schemes (like the standard sequential PINN architecture) can lead to unstable signal evolution, whereas implicit and higher-order schemes yield stable dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE.
The failure of a PINN to learn the inviscid Burgers' equation is linked to deviations from random matrix statistics and unstable signal propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the one-dimensional Burgers' equation and a specific PINN architecture (8 hidden layers, 100 neurons).
The connection between PINNs and (generalized) path integral solutions of PDEs is speculative and requires future exploration.
future_direction: Explore precise technical details of the connection between PINNs and path integral solutions of PDEs.
Extend the analysis to more complex PDEs and network architectures.
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often exhibit weight matrices that appear statistically random after training, yet their implications for signal propagation and stability remain unsatisfactorily understood, let alone the interpretability. In this work, we analyze the spectral and statistical properties of trained PINN weights using viscous and inviscid variants of the one-dimensional Burgers' equation, and show that the learned weights reside in a high-entropy regime consistent with predictions from random matrix theory. To investigate the dynamical consequences of such weight structures, we study the evolution of signal features inside a network through the lens of neural partial differential equations (neural PDEs). We show that random and structured weight matrices can be associated with specific discretizations of neural PDEs, and that the numerical stability of these discretizations governs the stability of signal propagation through the network. In particular, explicit unstable schemes lead to degraded signal evolution, whereas stable implicit and higher-order schemes yield well-behaved dynamics for the same underlying neural PDE. Our results offer an explicit example of how numerical stability and network architecture shape signal propagation in deep networks, in relation to random matrix and neural PDE descriptions in PINNs.

papers.title: GINN-KAN: Interpretability pipelining with applications in Physics Informed Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we create an interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN to overcome their individual limitations and be effectively applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GINN-KAN, a novel interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN, and demonstrates its application to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), creating interpretable PINNs that outperform black-box networks.
papers.conclusion: GINN-KAN represents a significant step forward in developing interpretable neural networks, offering a promising balance between interpretability and performance, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets.
GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform traditional PINNs with black-box networks on 15 different partial differential equations.
GINN struggles to learn non-Laurent polynomial (non-LP) equations, while KAN struggles to learn equations containing multiplicative terms.
GINN-KAN combines the strengths of both GINN and KAN, performing well on both LP and non-LP equations and on equations with multiplications.
GINN-KAN can be trained using backpropagation and integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal adjustments.
papers.limitation: GINN-KAN is restricted to inputs with positive values, a limitation inherited from GINN.
future_direction: Explore more robust architectures that maintain interpretability while overcoming the positive input limitation.
Develop better regularization techniques to enable GINN-KAN to accurately discover concise ground truth equations.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful function approximators, yet their ``black-box" nature often renders them opaque and difficult to interpret. While many post-hoc explanation methods exist, they typically fail to capture the underlying reasoning processes of the networks. A truly interpretable neural network would be trained similarly to conventional models using techniques such as backpropagation, but additionally provide insights into the learned input-output relationships. In this work, we introduce the concept of interpretability pipelineing, to incorporate multiple interpretability techniques to outperform each individual technique. To this end, we first evaluate several architectures that promise such interpretability, with a particular focus on two recent models selected for their potential to incorporate interpretability into standard neural network architectures while still leveraging backpropagation: the Growing Interpretable Neural Network (GINN) and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN). We analyze the limitations and strengths of each and introduce a novel interpretable neural network GINN-KAN that synthesizes the advantages of both models. When tested on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets, GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN. To highlight the capabilities and the generalizability of this approach, we position GINN-KAN as an alternative to conventional black-box networks in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). We expect this to have far-reaching implications in the application of deep learning pipelines in the natural sciences. Our experiments with this interpretable PINN on 15 different partial differential equations demonstrate that GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform PINNs with black-box networks in solving differential equations and surpass the capabilities of both GINN and KAN.

papers.title: Identification of state functions by physically-guided neural networks with physically-meaningful internal layers
papers.research_question: How to predict the input-output relation in a physical system while fulfilling physical constraints, and how to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Physically-Guided Neural Networks with Internal Variables (PGNNIV), a method that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to predict system behavior and infer internal state variables, showing improved convergence, data efficiency, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: PGNNIV is a promising framework that combines the predictive power of neural networks with physical interpretability, and shows advantages over standard neural networks in terms of convergence, data needs, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.key_findings:
The method accelerates the training process.
It reduces the amount of data required for similar accuracy.
It filters noise in experimental data.
It provides improved extrapolation capacity.
It allows obtaining internal state variables without additional assumptions.
papers.limitation:
For deep neural models, large and varied data are needed.
Defining successful network topology and hyperparameters is complex and time-consuming.
Predictions may not be as accurate as using full prescribed mathematical models.
papers.abstract: Substitution of well-grounded theoretical models by data-driven predictions is not as simple in engineering and sciences as it is in social and economic fields. Scientific problems suffer most times from paucity of data, while they may involve a large number of variables and parameters that interact in complex and non-stationary ways, obeying certain physical laws. Moreover, a physically-based model is not only useful for making predictions, but to gain knowledge by the interpretation of its structure, parameters, and mathematical properties. The solution to these shortcomings seems to be the seamless blending of the tremendous predictive power of the data-driven approach with the scientific consistency and interpretability of physically-based models. We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features
papers.research_question: Whether interpretable abstractions corresponding to physical features are present in the internal representations of data-driven physics models like GraphCast, and if these abstractions are physically consistent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable physical features from the internal activations of the data-driven weather model GraphCast, and that modifying these features leads to physically consistent changes in predictions, offering a window into the model's black-box behavior.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders applied to GraphCast extract highly interpretable physical features, and modifying these features allows probing of the model's internal abstractions, contributing to model trust and potential scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features in GraphCast corresponding to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal/seasonal patterns, precipitation, geographical coding, and sea-ice extent.
Features like sea-ice extent are learned dynamically even though not present in the model's input or output.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are identified, reflecting potential architecture bias.
Sparse probing identifies single features that strongly predict tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
Interventions that modify a tropical cyclone feature lead to interpretable and physically consistent changes in hurricane strength and evolution in the model's predictions.
papers.limitation:
The correlation between sea-ice features and actual ice extent is demonstrated, but a more rigorous causal analysis is needed for a complete account.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are spurious and potentially undesirable from an interpretability perspective.
ERA5 fields themselves are not in perfect hydrostatic balance, which affects the evaluation of physical consistency.
future_direction: Conduct more rigorous causal analysis of the discovered features.
Build mechanistic accounts for the interaction of features leading to model predictions.
Train specifically sparse models to have interpretable computations.
papers.abstract: Large data-driven physics models like DeepMind's weather model GraphCast have empirically succeeded in parameterizing time operators for complex dynamical systems with an accuracy reaching or in some cases exceeding that of traditional physics-based solvers. Unfortunately, how these data-driven models perform computations is largely unknown and whether their internal representations are interpretable or physically consistent is an open question. Here, we adapt tools from interpretability research in Large Language Models to analyze intermediate computational layers in GraphCast, leveraging sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable features in the neuron space of the model. We uncover distinct features on a wide range of length and time scales that correspond to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal behavior, large-scale precipitation patterns, specific geographical coding, and sea-ice extent, among others. We further demonstrate how the precise abstraction of these features can be probed via interventions on the prediction steps of the model. As a case study, we sparsely modify a feature corresponding to tropical cyclones in GraphCast and observe interpretable and physically consistent modifications to evolving hurricanes. Such methods offer a window into the black-box behavior of data-driven physics models and are a step towards realizing their potential as trustworthy predictors and scientifically valuable tools for discovery.

papers.title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
papers.research_question: How does the function space of training data affect the generalization of machine learning models when learning linear differential equations, and can learned models be interpreted in terms of Green's functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization in learning spatial physics depends critically on the function space of the training data, and introduces a cross-validation technique and a mechanistic interpretability lens based on extracting Green's functions from learned models.
papers.conclusion: Learning spatially dependent problems is limited by the underlying function space of the training data, and careful data selection and cross-validation are needed; different model classes exhibit opposing generalization behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Learned parameters in finite difference models converge with error depending on grid spacing and polynomial order of data.
Linear models only converge to a projection of the true operator onto the subspace of the training data, limiting out-of-distribution generalization.
Deep models and SciML models (DeepONet, Neural Operator) do not always generalize out-of-distribution.
Physics-informed losses (PINNs, PI-DeepONet) suffer from the same subspace limitation as black-box models.
Green's function operators can be extracted from black-box models when they generalize effectively across test domains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires a priori knowledge of how the dataset was constructed.
Real-world data collection has inherent limitations that may hinder discovering unknown physics.
future_direction: Develop new methods capable of discovering the underlying subspace of the data to compensate for limitations.
Use cross-set generalization as an evaluation benchmark for future differential equation learning techniques.
papers.abstract: While there are many applications of ML to scientific problems that look promising, visuals can be deceiving. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model. A similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models, including physics-specific techniques. Counterintuitively, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, which can serve as a benchmark.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: Physically Interpretable Representation and Controlled Generation for Turbulence Data
papers.research_question: How to extract meaningful latent representations from high-dimensional turbulence data while preserving physical structures for clustering and generative modeling?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a GMV AE framework for dimensionality reduction, clustering, and generative modeling of turbulence data, along with a novel quantitative metric for physical interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The GMV AE framework effectively addresses dimension reduction, clustering, and generative sampling while preserving global physical similarities, enabling interpretable latent representations for complex systems.
papers.key_findings:
GMV AE produces a more disenangled latent manifold compared to baseline methods like Isomap, UMAP, and VAE.
The latent manifold shows a smooth distribution of Reynolds numbers, encoding the continuous nature of fluid flow regimes.
The proposed interpretability metric validates the smoothness of physical quantities across the latent manifold.
GMV AE embeddings are robust to variations in the number of clusters when sufficiently large.
The framework enables conditional generation of flow data by mapping Reynolds numbers to latent embeddings.
future_direction: Extend GMV AE to multi-modal learning tasks by integrating diverse data sources and enabling cross-modal translation.
papers.abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays a pivotal role in fluid mechanics, enabling precise simulations of fluid behavior through partial differential equations (PDEs). However, traditional CFD methods are resource-intensive, particularly for high-fidelity simulations of complex flows, which are further complicated by high dimensionality, inherent stochasticity, and limited data availability. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a data-driven approach that leverages a Gaussian Mixture Variational Autoencoder (GMVAE) to encode high-dimensional scientific data into low-dimensional, physically meaningful representations. The GMVAE learns a structured latent space where data can be categorized based on physical properties such as the Reynolds number while maintaining global physical consistency. To assess the interpretability of the learned representations, we introduce a novel metric based on graph spectral theory, quantifying the smoothness of physical quantities along the latent manifold. We validate our approach using 2D Navier-Stokes simulations of flow past a cylinder over a range of Reynolds numbers. Our results demonstrate that the GMVAE provides improved clustering, meaningful latent structure, and robust generative capabilities compared to baseline dimensionality reduction methods. This framework offers a promising direction for data-driven turbulence modeling and broader applications in computational fluid dynamics and engineering systems.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: Physical Symmetries Embedded in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can physical constraints (such as symmetries and conservation laws) be embedded into neural network architectures to guarantee that predictions obey known physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture (hub layer) that embeds physical constraints (symmetries and conservation laws) exactly into the network structure, guaranteeing that predictions satisfy the underlying physics without the need for explicit regularization terms.
papers.conclusion: Embedding physical constraints into neural networks via hub layers improves predictive power, training efficiency, and robustness, and is crucial for reliable predictions in data-scarce regimes.
papers.key_findings:
A hub layer can enforce even/odd symmetry in regression tasks, outperforming standard MLPs in preserving symmetry while fitting noisy data.
For energy-conserving regression, a hub layer that corrects the MLP prediction using Hamiltonian dynamics ensures energy conservation and closed phase-space trajectories.
An unsupervised symplectic neural network, designed by embedding Hamilton's equations, conserves energy when solving differential equations and converges faster than a standard MLP.
future_direction: Embed other important symmetries into neural networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are a central technique in machine learning. Recent years have seen a wave of interest in applying neural networks to physical systems for which the governing dynamics are known and expressed through differential equations. Two fundamental challenges facing the development of neural networks in physics applications is their lack of interpretability and their physics-agnostic design. The focus of the present work is to embed physical constraints into the structure of the neural network to address the second fundamental challenge. By constraining tunable parameters (such as weights and biases) and adding special layers to the network, the desired constraints are guaranteed to be satisfied without the need for explicit regularization terms. This is demonstrated on upervised and unsupervised networks for two basic symmetries: even/odd symmetry of a function and energy conservation. In the supervised case, the network with embedded constraints is shown to perform well on regression problems while simultaneously obeying the desired constraints whereas a traditional network fits the data but violates the underlying constraints. Finally, a new unsupervised neural network is proposed that guarantees energy conservation through an embedded symplectic structure. The symplectic neural network is used to solve a system of energy-conserving differential equations and out-performs an unsupervised, non-symplectic neural network.

papers.title: Differentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator for Interpretable and Integrable Latent Space Modeling
papers.research_question: How to achieve interpretable latent space modeling in scientific machine learning by integrating differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DIANO, a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs interpretable latent spaces for dimensionality and geometric reduction, with integrated differentiable PDE solvers for physics-consistent temporal evolution.
papers.conclusion: DIANO demonstrates capability for interpretable and integrable latent space modeling, enabling dimensional and geometrical reduction with physics-based dynamics for complex spatio-temporal flows.
papers.key_findings:
DIANO produces interpretable latent vorticity structures with fewer Fourier modes, balancing reconstruction accuracy and interpretability.
DIANO enables temporal evolution of latent states using integrated PDE solvers, accurately predicting future flow fields.
The framework supports geometrical reduction from 2D to 1D, solving reduced PDEs in latent space and reconstructing to original geometry.
DIANO outperforms baseline models like CNO, CNN-AE, and NN-AE in terms of latent space interpretability and reconstruction error.
Solving lower-fidelity PDEs in latent space allows trade-offs between solver complexity, efficiency, and accuracy.
papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning has enabled the extraction of physical insights from high-dimensional spatiotemporal flow data using linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques. Despite these advances, achieving interpretability within the latent space remains a challenge. To address this, we propose the DIfferentiable Autoencoding Neural Operator (DIANO), a deterministic autoencoding neural operator framework that constructs physically interpretable latent spaces for both dimensional and geometric reduction, with the provision to enforce differential governing equations directly within the latent space. Built upon neural operators, DIANO compresses high-dimensional input functions into a low-dimensional latent space via spatial coarsening through an encoding neural operator and subsequently reconstructs the original inputs using a decoding neural operator through spatial refinement. We assess DIANO's latent space interpretability and performance in dimensionality reduction against baseline models, including the Convolutional Neural Operator and standard autoencoders. Furthermore, a fully differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solver is developed and integrated within the latent space, enabling the temporal advancement of both high- and low-fidelity PDEs, thereby embedding physical priors into the latent dynamics. We further investigate various PDE formulations, including the 2D unsteady advection-diffusion and the 3D Pressure-Poisson equation, to examine their influence on shaping the latent flow representations. Benchmark problems considered include flow past a 2D cylinder, flow through a 2D symmetric stenosed artery, and a 3D patient-specific coronary artery. These case studies demonstrate DIANO's capability to solve PDEs within a latent space that facilitates both dimensional and geometrical reduction while allowing latent interpretability.

papers.title: Controlling generative models with continuous factors of variations
papers.research_question: How to find interpretable directions in the latent space of generative models to control continuous factors of variations such as position and scale of objects in generated images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to find interpretable directions in the latent space of generative models that correspond to continuous factors of variations, enabling precise control over properties like object position and scale without human annotations.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method to extract meaningful directions in the latent space of generative models, enabling precise control over factors like translation and scale, which advances interpretability of latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can control horizontal and vertical position and scale of objects in generated images from BigGAN and β-VAE.
The directions for factors like position and scale are shared across different object categories in BigGAN.
In BigGAN, spatial factors of variation are mainly encoded in the first part of the hierarchical latent code.
Disentangled representations (achieved with higher β in β-VAE) lead to more precise control over factors.
The proposed reconstruction loss with frequency weighting produces sharper reconstructions and improves inversion of generative models.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on simple transformations like position and scale; more sophisticated transformations are not tested.
For large scales, the algorithm fails due to poor performance of the saliency model when the object covers almost the entire image.
future_direction: Adapt the method to other factors of variations such as rotations, brightness, contrast, color, or local deformations.
Use the method to analyze distributions of factors in training datasets to reveal potential bias.
papers.abstract: Recent deep generative models are able to provide photo-realistic images as well as visual or textual content embeddings useful to address various tasks of computer vision and natural language processing. Their usefulness is nevertheless often limited by the lack of control over the generative process or the poor understanding of the learned representation. To overcome these major issues, very recent work has shown the interest of studying the semantics of the latent space of generative models. In this paper, we propose to advance on the interpretability of the latent space of generative models by introducing a new method to find meaningful directions in the latent space of any generative model along which we can move to control precisely specific properties of the generated image like the position or scale of the object in the image. Our method does not require human annotations and is particularly well suited for the search of directions encoding simple transformations of the generated image, such as translation, zoom or color variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method qualitatively and quantitatively, both for GANs and variational auto-encoders.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems. Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Loss Jump During Loss Switch in Solving PDEs with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving partial differential equations (PDEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers and analyzes a loss-jump phenomenon during loss switching in PDE-solving neural networks, attributing it to different frequency preferences under different loss functions.
papers.conclusion: The loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.
papers.key_findings:
When switching the loss function from data loss to model loss, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately, a phenomenon termed loss jump.
The loss-jump phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions.
Theoretical analysis explains the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss.
papers.abstract: Using neural networks to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) is gaining popularity as an alternative approach in the scientific computing community. Neural networks can integrate different types of information into the loss function. These include observation data, governing equations, and variational forms, etc. These loss functions can be broadly categorized into two types: observation data loss directly constrains and measures the model output, while other loss functions indirectly model the performance of the network, which can be classified as model loss. However, this alternative approach lacks a thorough understanding of its underlying mechanisms, including theoretical foundations and rigorous characterization of various phenomena. This work focuses on investigating how different loss functions impact the training of neural networks for solving PDEs. We discover a stable loss-jump phenomenon: when switching the loss function from the data loss to the model loss, which includes different orders of derivative information, the neural network solution significantly deviates from the exact solution immediately. Further experiments reveal that this phenomenon arises from the different frequency preferences of neural networks under different loss functions. We theoretically analyze the frequency preference of neural networks under model loss. This loss-jump phenomenon provides a valuable perspective for examining the underlying mechanisms of neural networks in solving PDEs.

papers.title: Parametric PDE Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning and Differentiable L0-Sparse Polynomial Policies
papers.research_question: How can we learn sparse, interpretable, and generalizable control policies for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) using deep reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a deep reinforcement learning method with differentiable L0 regularization and dictionary learning to learn sparse, interpretable, and generalizable control policies for parametric PDEs.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully learns sparse, interpretable control policies for parametric PDEs that generalize to unseen parameters and are robust to noise.
papers.key_findings:
The L0-sparse polynomial TD3 agent outperforms baseline DNN-based TD3 and L1-sparse polynomial TD3 in terms of reward and cost.
The learned policies are interpretable and can be written as closed-form polynomial equations.
The policies generalize to unseen parameters of the PDE without retraining.
Sparse policies are more robust to noise on measurements.
papers.limitation: The number of polynomial features scales poorly with the dimension of the input and the degree of the polynomial.
future_direction: Extending the method with machine learning-based dimensionality reduction techniques such as autoencoders.
Exploring generalization capability and data-efficiency in more complex real-world dynamical systems.
papers.abstract: Optimal control of parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) is crucial in many applications in engineering and science. In recent years, the progress in scientific machine learning has opened up new frontiers for the control of parametric PDEs. In particular, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has the potential to solve high-dimensional and complex control problems in a large variety of applications. Most DRL methods rely on deep neural network (DNN) control policies. However, for many dynamical systems, DNN-based control policies tend to be over-parametrized, which means they need large amounts of training data, show limited robustness, and lack interpretability. In this work, we leverage dictionary learning and differentiable L$_0$ regularization to learn sparse, robust, and interpretable control policies for parametric PDEs. Our sparse policy architecture is agnostic to the DRL method and can be used in different policy-gradient and actor-critic DRL algorithms without changing their policy-optimization procedure. We test our approach on the challenging tasks of controlling parametric Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and convection-diffusion-reaction PDEs. We show that our method (1) outperforms baseline DNN-based DRL policies, (2) allows for the derivation of interpretable equations of the learned optimal control laws, and (3) generalizes to unseen parameters of the PDE without retraining the policies.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Interpreted machine learning in fluid dynamics: explaining relaminarisation events in wall-bounded shear flows
papers.research_question: How can the SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) algorithm be used to interpret machine learning models in fluid dynamics, specifically to identify which flow features are important for predicting relaminarisation events?
papers.core_contribution: Applies SHAP to fluid dynamics, demonstrating it can identify physically interpretable features important for predicting relaminarisation events, and suggests that streak instabilities are key to the break-up of the self-sustaining cycle.
papers.conclusion: SHAP values can identify significant features for predicting relaminarisation events in wall-bounded shear flows, providing physical insights into the self-sustaining process.
papers.key_findings:
For the nine-mode model, SHAP identifies the laminar profile, streamwise vortex, and a specific sinusoidal streak instability as the most important features for predicting relaminarisation events.
The streak mode itself is not identified as important, likely because it is strongly correlated with the vortex mode and thus provides little additional information.
For DNS data of plane Couette flow, SHAP indicates the classifier bases its decisions on regions in the flow associated with streak instabilities.
SHAP can be successfully applied to larger fluid dynamics datasets, providing human-interpretable insight.
The method shows that well-performing classifiers are required for effective explanation, as feature importance metrics decrease with declining prediction accuracy.
future_direction: Extension to higher-dimensional data from experiments or high-resolution numerical simulations.
Application to other flow configurations and dynamical systems.
Incorporation of time-dependent SHAP values to capture dynamical evolution.
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is becoming increasingly popular in fluid dynamics. Powerful ML algorithms such as neural networks or ensemble methods are notoriously difficult to interpret. Here, we introduce the novel Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) algorithm (Lundberg & Lee, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems , 2017, pp. 4765–4774), a game-theoretic approach that explains the output of a given ML model in the fluid dynamics context. We give a proof of concept concerning SHAP as an explainable artificial intelligence method providing useful and human-interpretable insight for fluid dynamics. To show that the feature importance ranking provided by SHAP can be interpreted physically, we first consider data from an established low-dimensional model based on the self-sustaining process (SSP) in wall-bounded shear flows, where each data feature has a clear physical and dynamical interpretation in terms of known representative features of the near-wall dynamics, i.e. streamwise vortices, streaks and linear streak instabilities. SHAP determines consistently that only the laminar profile, the streamwise vortex and a specific streak instability play a major role in the prediction. We demonstrate that the method can be applied to larger fluid dynamics datasets by a SHAP evaluation on plane Couette flow in a minimal flow unit focussing on the relevance of streaks and their instabilities for the prediction of relaminarisation events. Here, we find that the prediction is based on proxies for streak modulations corresponding to linear streak instabilities within the SSP. That is, the SHAP analysis suggests that the break-up of the self-sustaining cycle is connected with a suppression of streak instabilities.

papers.title: Interpreting CFD Surrogates through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the latent representations of graph-based CFD surrogate models to enhance explainability and trustworthiness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a post-hoc interpretability framework for graph-based CFD surrogate models using sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable latent features that correspond to physical flow structures.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoding is a practical and effective tool for explaining graph surrogates in fluid dynamics, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE yields interpretable and physically meaningful representations aligned with phenomena like vorticity or flow structures.
Global and time-local salient coordinates show temporal consistency, with variance and mean-absolute metrics capturing coherent features.
Mesh-space visualization reveals that aggregated latent activity hierarchically expands from cylinder surface to wake, mirroring physical importance.
Individual latent dimensions specialize in distinct flow structures, confirming disentanglement of physical phenomena.
SAE-based saliency consistently outperforms baselines like embedding-norm and PCA in aligning with high-vorticity regions.
papers.abstract: Learning-based surrogate models have become a practical alternative to high-fidelity CFD solvers, but their latent representations remain opaque and hinder adoption in safety-critical or regulation-bound settings. This work introduces a posthoc interpretability framework for graph-based surrogate models used in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) by leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By obtaining an overcomplete basis in the node embedding space of a pretrained surrogate, the method extracts a dictionary of interpretable latent features. The approach enables the identification of monosemantic concepts aligned with physical phenomena such as vorticity or flow structures, offering a model-agnostic pathway to enhance explainability and trustworthiness in CFD applications.

papers.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Autoregressive Deep Learning: Or, Examining Temporal Decay of Gradient Coherence
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish between genuine generalization and mere memorization in autoregressive PDE emulators? What are the limitations of standard models and training routines in achieving generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces influence-based diagnostics to show that autoregressive PDE emulators fail to learn a globally consistent solution operator, instead memorizing time- and class-specific patterns, and provides insights for improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current physics-agnostic PDE emulators fail to internalize the governing equations, and influence functions provide a diagnostic framework to distinguish memorization from generalization, highlighting the need for physics-based constraints or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive PDE emulators exhibit rapid decay of off-diagonal influence, indicating gradient responses are localized in time and class.
Both UNet and ViT models fail to support nontrivial off-diagonal response, meaning they do not learn a shared feature basis across trajectories.
Gradient geometry is class-locked, with limited inter-class influence, showing that models treat different initial conditions as separate tasks.
The neural tangent kernel spectrum reveals a stiff, anisotropic geometry, indicating that low test error coexists with sharp, high-curvature directions rather than robust generalization.
The models behave as statistical estimators that interpolate within neighborhoods of the training data, rather than learning the underlying physical laws.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based constraints as regularizers or architectural biases to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained as autoregressive PDE surrogates hold significant promise for accelerating scientific discovery through their capacity to both extrapolate beyond training regimes and efficiently adapt to downstream tasks despite a paucity of examples for fine-tuning. However, reliably achieving genuine generalization - a necessary capability for producing novel scientific insights and robustly performing during deployment - remains a critical challenge. Establishing whether or not these requirements are met demands evaluation metrics capable of clearly distinguishing genuine model generalization from mere memorization. We apply the influence function formalism to systematically characterize how autoregressive PDE surrogates assimilate and propagate information derived from diverse physical scenarios, revealing fundamental limitations of standard models and training routines in addition to providing actionable insights regarding the design of improved surrogates.

papers.title: Loss Landscape Geometry and the Learning of Symmetries: Or, What Influence Functions Reveal About Robust Generalization
papers.research_question: Do neural emulators of PDE solution operators internalize physical symmetries, and how can we diagnose this through learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an influence-based diagnostic that measures gradient coherence across symmetry orbits to determine whether neural PDE emulators have internalized physical symmetries, linking it to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed influence-based diagnostic reveals that gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is essential for robust generalization, providing a tool to assess whether models truly learn physics or just fit data.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is necessary for models to generalize over symmetry transformations.
Models can achieve low test error without learning symmetries, indicated by weak gradient coherence.
UNets and ViTs exhibit different patterns of gradient coherence: UNets show more uniform coupling, while ViTs concentrate influence on a subset of symmetry transformations.
Symmetry breaking in forward passes corresponds to suppressed cross-influence in the loss landscape.
The diagnostic can be used to evaluate symmetry learning and guide data augmentation.
papers.limitation:
Certain physically relevant symmetries (Galilean boosts, scaling) are not studied.
Empirical analysis is limited to UNet and ViT architectures.
Diagnostics characterize symmetry learning relative to the training distribution; when symmetry transformations are poorly represented in data, influence-based measures reflect this bias.
future_direction: Extending the influence-based analysis to probe the response under small Galilean boosts.
Development of approximate or relaxed symmetry mechanisms that retain structure to guide generalization while preserving optimization flexibility.
papers.abstract: We study how neural emulators of partial differential equation solution operators internalize physical symmetries by introducing an influence-based diagnostic that measures the propagation of parameter updates between symmetry-related states, defined as the metric-weighted overlap of loss gradients evaluated along group orbits. This quantity probes the local geometry of the learned loss landscape and goes beyond forward-pass equivariance tests by directly assessing whether learning dynamics couple physically equivalent configurations. Applying our diagnostic to autoregressive fluid flow emulators, we show that orbit-wise gradient coherence provides the mechanism for learning to generalize over symmetry transformations and indicates when training selects a symmetry compatible basin. The result is a novel technique for evaluating if surrogate models have internalized symmetry properties of the known solution operator.

papers.title: A reproducing kernel framework for interpretable parameter estimation and learning in dynamical systems
papers.research_question: How can explainable machine learning models be used for accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation in dynamical systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework combining explainable machine learning models with SHAP-based interpretability for parameter estimation in dynamical systems, demonstrating accurate, interpretable, and efficient estimation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature-based learning framework for parameter estimation in differential equation systems combines predictive modeling with post-hoc explainability, with kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) achieving higher predictive accuracy and robustness compared to neural network baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel-based methods (KRR and GPR) consistently outperformed neural network models (MLP and CNN) in parameter estimation accuracy.
Statistical features extracted from trajectories were more informative for parameter estimation than frequency-domain or spectrogram features.
SHAP-based feature attribution revealed consistent feature importance rankings across different model types, indicating robust feature-to-parameter relationships.
The proposed framework achieves accurate parameter estimation while providing transparency into the inference process through explainability techniques.
The integration of simulation-based dataset generation, feature extraction, and interpretable modeling offers a new perspective for combining machine learning with domain-specific modeling.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical analysis is needed to formalize the connection between system dynamics and feature relevance.
Validation has been limited to synthetic datasets; extending to real-world data is important for broader practical applicability.
Current kernel-based methods do not scale efficiently, and neural architectures require larger datasets to fully leverage their capacity, indicating scalability and data volume limitations.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to stable multi-parameter estimation.
Develop data-driven techniques for identifying informative parameter ranges.
Design adaptive dataset generation strategies to improve training efficiency and interpretability.
