papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate a suite of explainable machine learning models -- including Kernel Ridge Regression, Gaussian Process Regression, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Multi-Layer Perceptrons -- for parameter inference in systems of differential equations. By combining these models with explainability techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations, we extract explicit feature-to-parameter mappings, offering deeper insight into the inference process. Building on these insights, we propose lightweight, hand-engineered estimators that approximate parameter estimation tasks without requiring complex optimization. Additionally, we introduce a systematic methodology for dataset generation, incorporating time-series simulation and diverse feature extraction. Our results demonstrate that explainability-driven modeling can achieve accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient parameter estimation, offering a new perspective on the integration of machine learning with domain-specific modeling.

papers.title: How does My Model Fail? Automatic Identification and Interpretation of Physical Plausibility Failure Modes with Matryoshka Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we automatically identify and interpret specific physical plausibility error patterns in generative models to enable targeted model improvements?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce Matryoshka Transcoders, a framework for automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features in generative models via hierarchical sparse feature learning on classifier representations, enabling interpretable benchmarking and failure mode analysis.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka Transcoders enable automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features, providing a hierarchical sparse feature learning approach that reveals systematic failure modes across generative models and paves the way for targeted improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka Transcoders outperform baseline methods (SAE, Matryoshka SAE, Transcoder) in both population-based and description-based feature relevance metrics.
The method discovers diverse physical plausibility failure modes (e.g., anatomical distortions, malformed text, implausible styles) and attaches accurate natural language descriptions.
Benchmarking eight generative models reveals FLUX achieves the best physical plausibility (lowest mean error count) while SDXL-turbo exhibits the most violations.
A feature relevance bottleneck phenomenon is observed where features cluster at two extremes (70-80% and >95% relevance), justifying focus on highly selective features.
Smaller dictionary sizes yield more focused and relevant features, while larger sizes provide broader coverage, motivating the use of nested dictionaries.
papers.limitation:
Discovered features are not yet incorporated into training pipelines to actively reduce physical plausibility failures.
Certain subtle or rare physical violations may be underrepresented if training data lacks sufficient examples, creating potential evaluation blind spots.
The feature absorption phenomenon is not quantified for visual inputs due to the high-dimensional, continuous nature of image representations.
The framework focuses only on physical plausibility, leaving other quality dimensions (aesthetics, semantic faithfulness, social biases) for future work.
future_direction: Incorporating discovered features into training pipelines to actively reduce physical plausibility failures.
Developing methods to measure feature absorption rate in vision models.
Extending the framework to other quality dimensions such as aesthetics, semantic faithfulness, and social biases.
papers.abstract: Although recent generative models are remarkably capable of producing instruction-following and realistic outputs, they remain prone to notable physical plausibility failures. Though critical in applications, these physical plausibility errors often escape detection by existing evaluation methods. Furthermore, no framework exists for automatically identifying and interpreting specific physical error patterns in natural language, preventing targeted model improvements. We introduce Matryoshka Transcoders, a novel framework for the automatic discovery and interpretation of physical plausibility features in generative models. Our approach extends the Matryoshka representation learning paradigm to transcoder architectures, enabling hierarchical sparse feature learning at multiple granularity levels. By training on intermediate representations from a physical plausibility classifier and leveraging large multimodal models for interpretation, our method identifies diverse physics-related failure modes without manual feature engineering, achieving superior feature relevance and feature accuracy compared to existing approaches. We utilize the discovered visual patterns to establish a benchmark for evaluating physical plausibility in generative models. Our analysis of eight state-of-the-art generative models provides valuable insights into how these models fail to follow physical constraints, paving the way for further model improvements.

papers.title: Nonlocal Attention Operator: Materializing Hidden Knowledge Towards Interpretable Physics Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we design an attention-based neural operator that simultaneously solves forward and inverse PDE problems, providing interpretability and generalizability to unseen physical systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), a novel neural operator architecture that uses an attention-based kernel map to simultaneously solve forward (modeling) and inverse (discovery) PDE problems, offering interpretability and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.conclusion: NAO is an effective neural operator architecture for simultaneously learning forward and inverse PDE solvers from data, providing interpretability through the discovered kernel and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
NAO achieves lower operator and kernel errors compared to discrete and softmax attention variants in forward and inverse PDE tasks.
NAO generalizes to unseen physical systems (zero-shot learning) and across different data resolutions.
The attention mechanism acts as a data-driven regularizer, resolving the ill-posedness of inverse PDE problems by exploring a function space of identifiability.
NAO's kernel map provides interpretability by revealing the hidden physical mechanism (kernel) from data.
NAO outperforms baseline models (Discrete-NAO, Softmax-NAO, NAO-u, AFNO, Autoencoder) in terms of generalizability and accuracy.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on learning from a small to medium number (<500) of similar physical systems due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Expand the coverage to enable learning across different types of physical systems.
Build a foundation model in scientific machine learning.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent popularity of attention-based neural architectures in core AI fields like natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), their potential in modeling complex physical systems remains under-explored. Learning problems in physical systems are often characterized as discovering operators that map between function spaces based on a few instances of function pairs. This task frequently presents a severely ill-posed PDE inverse problem. In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture based on the attention mechanism, which we coin Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), and explore its capability towards developing a foundation physical model. In particular, we show that the attention mechanism is equivalent to a double integral operator that enables nonlocal interactions among spatial tokens, with a data-dependent kernel characterizing the inverse mapping from data to the hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. As such, the attention mechanism extracts global prior information from training data generated by multiple systems, and suggests the exploratory space in the form of a nonlinear kernel map. Consequently, NAO can address ill-posedness and rank deficiency in inverse PDE problems by encoding regularization and achieving generalizability. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of NAO over baseline neural models in terms of generalizability to unseen data resolutions and system states. Our work not only suggests a novel neural operator architecture for learning interpretable foundation models of physical systems, but also offers a new perspective towards understanding the attention mechanism. Our code and data accompanying this paper are available at https://github.com/fishmoon1234/NAO.

papers.title: Using explainability to design physics-aware CNNs for solving subsurface inverse problems
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques be used to design physics-aware convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for solving subsurface inverse problems?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for using explainability techniques (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) to iteratively select CNN hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size, network depth) to develop physics-aware models for subsurface imaging that maintain high predictive accuracy while improving descriptive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that explainability methods (Score-CAM and Deep SHAP) can be used to iteratively tune CNN hyperparameters, leading to physics-aware models with high descriptive accuracy without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Initial deep CNNs (Transpose Convolution and Dense networks) had good predictive accuracy but low descriptive accuracy, as they focused on non-physical, low-power regions in the input dispersion images.
Changing the kernel size from 3x3 to 3x1 in deep networks did not significantly change predictive accuracy but showed slightly better descriptive accuracy.
Reducing network depth (shallow networks) improved descriptive accuracy, with the shallow 3x1 kernel network focusing primarily on the physically meaningful high-power modal trend in the dispersion images.
The shallow 3x1 kernel CNN is recommended as it achieves high descriptive accuracy (making logical, physics-aware predictions) without a considerable loss in predictive accuracy.
papers.limitation: The shallow network recommended is sensitive to noisy inputs and may require additional denoising layers for field applications.
future_direction: Adding denoising layers to the shallow network for robustness to noisy field data.
Extending the framework to tune more hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: We present a novel method of using explainability techniques to design physics-aware neural networks. We demonstrate our approach by developing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for solving an inverse problem for shallow subsurface imaging. Although CNNs have gained popularity in recent years across many fields, the development of CNNs remains an art, as there are no clear guidelines regarding the selection of hyperparameters that will yield the best network. While optimization algorithms may be used to select hyperparameters automatically, these methods focus on developing networks with high predictive accuracy while disregarding model explainability (descriptive accuracy). However, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) addresses the absence of model explainability by providing tools that allow developers to evaluate the internal logic of neural networks. In this study, we use the explainability methods Score-CAM and Deep SHAP to select hyperparameters, such as kernel sizes and network depth, to develop a physics-aware CNN for shallow subsurface imaging. We begin with a relatively deep Encoder-Decoder network, which uses surface wave dispersion images as inputs and generates 2D shear wave velocity subsurface images as outputs. Through model explanations, we ultimately find that a shallow CNN using two convolutional layers with an atypical kernel size of 3x1 yields comparable predictive accuracy but with increased descriptive accuracy. We also show that explainability methods can be used to evaluate the network's complexity and decision-making. We believe this method can be used to develop neural networks with high predictive accuracy while also providing inherent explainability.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Experts Operator Transformer for Large-Scale PDE Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How to design a pre-training architecture for neural operators that efficiently scales model capacity while handling heterogeneous PDE datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MoE-POT, a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture for neural operator pre-training that efficiently scales model capacity and handles heterogeneous PDE datasets by dynamically routing inputs to specialized experts.
papers.conclusion: MoE-POT is an effective sparse architecture for PDE pre-training, achieving state-of-the-art performance and providing interpretability through the router's dataset classification ability.
papers.key_findings:
MoE-POT with 90M activated parameters achieves up to a 40% reduction in zero-shot error compared to existing models with 120M activated parameters.
The trained router-gating network can infer the PDE type of input data with 98% accuracy, validating the MoE architecture's ability to handle diverse datasets.
MoE-POT demonstrates better scaling laws and inference efficiency compared to dense models, with lower inference time for comparable total parameters.
The model shows strong performance on downstream tasks after fine-tuning, indicating effective transfer of pre-trained knowledge.
The architecture mitigates negative transfer from heterogeneous data mixing, maintaining stable performance as more diverse datasets are added during pre-training.
papers.limitation: The mathematical essence of the classification mechanism in the router-gating network has not been analyzed.
future_direction: Exploring how PDE classification can guide the construction of more effective pre-training datasets.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has proven effective in addressing data scarcity and performance limitations in solving PDE problems with neural operators. However, challenges remain due to the heterogeneity of PDE datasets in equation types, which leads to high errors in mixed training. Additionally, dense pre-training models that scale parameters by increasing network width or depth incur significant inference costs. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts Pre-training Operator Transformer (MoE-POT), a sparse-activated architecture that scales parameters efficiently while controlling inference costs. Specifically, our model adopts a layer-wise router-gating network to dynamically select 4 routed experts from 16 expert networks during inference, enabling the model to focus on equation-specific features. Meanwhile, we also integrate 2 shared experts, aiming to capture common properties of PDE and reduce redundancy among routed experts. The final output is computed as the weighted average of the results from all activated experts. We pre-train models with parameters from 30M to 0.5B on 6 public PDE datasets. Our model with 90M activated parameters achieves up to a 40% reduction in zero-shot error compared with existing models with 120M activated parameters. Additionally, we conduct interpretability analysis, showing that dataset types can be inferred from router-gating network decisions, which validates the rationality and effectiveness of the MoE architecture.

papers.title: On the flow matching interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we make the intermediate steps of flow matching models interpretable by constraining them to traverse physically meaningful states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to make flow matching interpretable by constraining each flow step to correspond to equilibrium states of a physical process, demonstrated on the 2D Ising model where steps represent thermal transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper addresses the challenge of interpreting diffusion steps in flow-matching models by constraining trajectories to physically meaningful transitions, demonstrating preserved physical fidelity with computational speedups over Monte Carlo methods and correct capture of phase transitions and critical phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed for larger lattices.
Each vector field update represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space.
The learned decoder generates configurations that closely resemble true physical behavior, especially near the critical temperature.
The method correctly captures phase transitions and critical phenomena.
The approach transforms abstract flow evolution into concrete, physically-grounded dynamics.
future_direction: Applying the framework to different diffusion models and other physical systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models based on flow matching have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet they suffer from a fundamental limitation: the lack of interpretability in their intermediate generation steps. In fact these models learn to transform noise into data through a series of vector field updates, however the meaning of each step remains opaque. We address this problem by proposing a general framework constraining each flow step to be sampled from a known physical distribution. Flow trajectories are mapped to (and constrained to traverse) the equilibrium states of the simulated physical process. We implement this approach through the 2D Ising model in such a way that flow steps become thermal equilibrium points along a parametric cooling schedule. Our proposed architecture includes an encoder that maps discrete Ising configurations into a continuous latent space, a flow-matching network that performs temperature-driven diffusion, and a projector that returns to discrete Ising states while preserving physical constraints. We validate this framework across multiple lattice sizes, showing that it preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed as the lattice size increases. In contrast with standard flow matching, each vector field represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space. This demonstrates that embedding physical semantics into generative flows transforms opaque neural trajectories into interpretable physical processes.

papers.title: How Learnable Grids Recover Fine Detail in Low Dimensions: A Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis of Multigrid Parametric Encodings
papers.research_question: Why do multigrid parametric encodings (MPEs) often outperform Fourier feature encodings (FFEs) in learning high-frequency details in low-dimensional mappings, and how does the structure of MPEs affect the neural tangent kernel (NTK) spectrum?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that multigrid parametric encodings (MPEs) improve a network's ability to learn high-frequency details by raising the eigenvalue spectrum of the neural tangent kernel (NTK), and that this improvement stems from the learnable grid structure rather than just the embedding space, unlike Fourier feature encodings (FFEs).
papers.conclusion: MPEs mitigate spectral bias in a fundamentally different way than FFEs by leveraging learnable grid parameters to raise the NTK eigenvalue spectrum, enabling better learning of high-frequency details in low-dimensional mappings.
papers.key_findings:
MPEs increase the minimum eigenvalue of the NTK by 8 orders of magnitude over the baseline MLP and 2 orders of magnitude over the FFE, corresponding to significant gains in PSNR and MS-SSIM.
The performance improvement of MPEs is isolated to their learnable grid parameters, not the embedding space, which is fundamentally different from FFEs that rely solely on the embedding.
The eigenvalue spectrum of the NTK is a reliable predictor of a network's ability to learn high-frequency details, with higher spectra leading to better performance.
MPEs outperform FFEs in learning fine details in both 2D image regression and 3D implicit surface regression tasks.
The NTK spectrum remains relatively stable during the latter half of training, validating its use for analysis.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not account for the influence of different activation functions.
The space of possible problems is too large to compute the NTK for each application.
future_direction: Optimizing encodings for specific applications by adjusting the interpolation kernel or tuning hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Neural networks that map between low dimensional spaces are ubiquitous in computer graphics and scientific computing; however, in their naive implementation, they are unable to learn high frequency information. We present a comprehensive analysis comparing the two most common techniques for mitigating this spectral bias: Fourier feature encodings (FFE) and multigrid parametric encodings (MPE). FFEs are seen as the standard for low dimensional mappings, but MPEs often outperform them and learn representations with higher resolution and finer detail. FFE's roots in the Fourier transform, make it susceptible to aliasing if pushed too far, while MPEs, which use a learned grid structure, have no such limitation. To understand the difference in performance, we use the neural tangent kernel (NTK) to evaluate these encodings through the lens of an analogous kernel regression. By finding a lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue of the NTK, we prove that MPEs improve a network's performance through the structure of their grid and not their learnable embedding. This mechanism is fundamentally different from FFEs, which rely solely on their embedding space to improve performance. Results are empirically validated on a 2D image regression task using images taken from 100 synonym sets of ImageNet and 3D implicit surface regression on objects from the Stanford graphics dataset. Using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and multiscale structural similarity (MS-SSIM) to evaluate how well fine details are learned, we show that the MPE increases the minimum eigenvalue by 8 orders of magnitude over the baseline and 2 orders of magnitude over the FFE. The increase in spectrum corresponds to a 15 dB (PSNR) / 0.65 (MS-SSIM) increase over baseline and a 12 dB (PSNR) / 0.33 (MS-SSIM) increase over the FFE.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Additive-feature-attribution methods: a review on explainable artificial intelligence for fluid dynamics and heat transfer
papers.core_contribution: This review paper summarizes the application of additive-feature-attribution methods (SHAP) in fluid dynamics and heat transfer, highlighting their importance for interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models.
papers.conclusion: This review shows that explainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.
papers.key_findings:
Additive-feature-attribution methods are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in fluid mechanics.
SHAP values provide a unique solution for understanding the model by linking input features with the model prediction.
The review categorizes applications into turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer.
papers.abstract: The use of data-driven methods in fluid mechanics has surged dramatically in recent years due to their capacity to adapt to the complex and multi-scale nature of turbulent flows, as well as to detect patterns in large-scale simulations or experimental tests. In order to interpret the relationships generated in the models during the training process, numerical attributions need to be assigned to the input features. One important example are the additive-feature-attribution methods. These explainability methods link the input features with the model prediction, providing an interpretation based on a linear formulation of the models. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP values) are formulated as the only possible interpretation that offers a unique solution for understanding the model. In this manuscript, the additive-feature-attribution methods are presented, showing four common implementations in the literature: kernel SHAP, tree SHAP, gradient SHAP, and deep SHAP. Then, the main applications of the additive-feature-attribution methods are introduced, dividing them into three main groups: turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer. This review shows thatexplainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Latent Abstractions in Generative Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How do diffusion-based generative models produce high-dimensional data by implicitly relying on a low-dimensional set of latent abstractions that guide the generative process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a novel theoretical framework based on Nonlinear Filtering that explains how diffusion models implicitly rely on latent abstractions to guide the generative process, and validates it empirically.
papers.conclusion: The Nonlinear Filtering framework offers a theoretical understanding of how diffusion models leverage latent abstractions, and experiments confirm the hierarchical emergence of these abstractions during generation.
papers.key_findings:
Latent abstractions emerge hierarchically in diffusion models, with global attributes (e.g., shape, wall hue) emerging before local details.
Mutual information between the generative process and latent abstractions increases over time, validating the theoretical framework.
The forking protocol demonstrates that once a latent factor emerges, different generative pathways converge to coherent values for that factor.
Linear probing on internal features of the denoising network reveals that latent abstractions are discernible even at high noise levels.
The theory provides a unified perspective on forward and backward diffusion processes as a single Nonlinear Filtering simulation.
papers.limitation: The theoretical framework requires technical assumptions and may encounter singularities at the final time T in the SDE dynamics.
future_direction: Applications in image editing and improved conditional generation.
papers.abstract: In this work we study how diffusion-based generative models produce high-dimensional data, such as an image, by implicitly relying on a manifestation of a low-dimensional set of latent abstractions, that guide the generative process. We present a novel theoretical framework that extends NLF, and that offers a unique perspective on SDE-based generative models. The development of our theory relies on a novel formulation of the joint (state and measurement) dynamics, and an information-theoretic measure of the influence of the system state on the measurement process. According to our theory, diffusion models can be cast as a system of SDE, describing a non-linear filter in which the evolution of unobservable latent abstractions steers the dynamics of an observable measurement process (corresponding to the generative pathways). In addition, we present an empirical study to validate our theory and previous empirical results on the emergence of latent abstractions at different stages of the generative process.

papers.title: FIGNN: Feature-Specific Interpretability for Graph Neural Network Surrogate Models
papers.research_question: How can we design a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that provides feature-specific interpretability for multivariate prediction tasks on unstructured grids in scientific applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-specific interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN) architecture with independent Top-K pooling masks per output variable and an error-budget regularization term to align interpretability with predictive error, enabling localized, feature-wise attribution in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.conclusion: FIGNN provides a balance between interpretability and predictive performance, offering domain experts detailed insights into feature-specific contributions to prediction accuracy in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.key_findings:
FIGNN provides feature-specific interpretability masks that highlight physically meaningful spatial regions for each predicted variable, such as frontal boundaries in climate data and recirculation zones in fluid flow.
The error budget regularization effectively localizes prediction errors within the masked regions, with stronger regularization increasing error concentration at the cost of slightly reduced predictive accuracy.
FIGNN maintains competitive predictive performance compared to baseline GNN models on both atmospheric (SPEEDY) and fluid dynamics (BFS) datasets.
The method generalizes across distinct physical domains (climate and fluid dynamics) with different mesh types and governing equations.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence and error localization) and predictive accuracy, controllable via the regularization parameter λ.
papers.limitation:
Error accumulation in multi-step rollouts leads to deteriorating prediction quality over long time horizons.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence) and predictive accuracy, where higher regularization improves error localization but increases final loss.
future_direction: Extending the framework to spatially three-dimensional settings.
Real-time adaptive interpretability.
Uncertainty quantification strategies.
Using FIGNN for inverse problems like super-resolution, control, and optimization.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel graph neural network (GNN) architecture, the Feature-specific Interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN), designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning surrogate models defined on unstructured grids in scientific applications. Traditional GNNs often obscure the distinct spatial influences of different features in multivariate prediction tasks. FIGNN addresses this limitation by introducing a feature-specific pooling strategy, which enables independent attribution of spatial importance for each predicted variable. Additionally, a mask-based regularization term is incorporated into the training objective to explicitly encourage alignment between interpretability and predictive error, promoting localized attribution of model performance. The method is evaluated for surrogate modeling of two physically distinct systems: the SPEEDY atmospheric circulation model and the backward-facing step (BFS) fluid dynamics benchmark. Results demonstrate that FIGNN achieves competitive predictive performance while revealing physically meaningful spatial patterns unique to each feature. Analysis of rollout stability, feature-wise error budgets, and spatial mask overlays confirm the utility of FIGNN as a general-purpose framework for interpretable surrogate modeling in complex physical domains.

papers.title: Multiscale Graph Neural Network Autoencoders for Interpretable Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop an autoencoder-based model that achieves both latent space interpretability and compatibility with unstructured meshes for complex fluid flow applications?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a novel graph neural network autoencoder that uses adaptive Top-K pooling to create interpretable latent graphs (visualized as masked fields) and multiscale message passing layers to efficiently reconstruct flow fields from unstructured mesh data.
papers.conclusion: The developed GNN autoencoder provides an interpretable and mesh-compatible framework for scientific machine learning, effectively identifying coherent flow structures and reconstructing flow fields, with promising potential for reduced-order modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The inclusion of multiscale message passing (MMP) layers, especially with coarsening in both encoder and decoder, significantly improves flow field reconstruction accuracy from the latent graph.
The latent graphs produced by the Top-K pooling layer (visualized as masked fields) identify time-evolving coherent structures in the flow, such as recirculation zones, providing direct physical interpretability.
Increasing the level of graph reduction (compression) leads to higher reconstruction errors, but the masked fields show how the model adapts its focus, e.g., shifting attention to inflow/outflow boundaries at high compression.
Reconstruction errors (RMSE) are more sensitive to Reynolds number for the streamwise velocity component compared to the vertical velocity component.
The architecture successfully handles unstructured meshes and complex geometries inherent to computational fluid dynamics simulations.
papers.limitation:
The effects of increased message passing and coarsening operations within the MMP layer warrant further investigation to potentially alleviate increased reconstruction error in higher-compression models.
Geometry extrapolation capability (performance on unseen geometric configurations) was not explored in this work.
future_direction: Investigating the effects of increased message passing and coarsening operations within the MMP layer.
Assessment of latent graph properties and model performance on different geometric configurations to solidify general applicability.
Using the concept of masked field evolution for interpretable data-based surrogate modeling of complex fluid flow phenomena.
papers.abstract: The goal of this work is to address two limitations in autoencoder-based models: latent space interpretability and compatibility with unstructured meshes. This is accomplished here with the development of a novel graph neural network (GNN) autoencoding architecture with demonstrations on complex fluid flow applications. To address the first goal of interpretability, the GNN autoencoder achieves reduction in the number nodes in the encoding stage through an adaptive graph reduction procedure. This reduction procedure essentially amounts to flowfield-conditioned node sampling and sensor identification, and produces interpretable latent graph representations tailored to the flowfield reconstruction task in the form of so-called masked fields. These masked fields allow the user to (a) visualize where in physical space a given latent graph is active, and (b) interpret the time-evolution of the latent graph connectivity in accordance with the time-evolution of unsteady flow features (e.g. recirculation zones, shear layers) in the domain. To address the goal of unstructured mesh compatibility, the autoencoding architecture utilizes a series of multi-scale message passing (MMP) layers, each of which models information exchange among node neighborhoods at various lengthscales. The MMP layer, which augments standard single-scale message passing with learnable coarsening operations, allows the decoder to more efficiently reconstruct the flowfield from the identified regions in the masked fields. Analysis of latent graphs produced by the autoencoder for various model settings are conducted using using unstructured snapshot data sourced from large-eddy simulations in a backward-facing step (BFS) flow configuration with an OpenFOAM-based flow solver at high Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Steering Along Manifolds to Control Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What if the concept being manipulated in a neural network's representations isn't on a straight line, and how can steering along manifolds provide better control than linear steering?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that steering along manifolds in representation space provides better control of neural network behavior than linear steering, and reveals alignment between representation geometry and behavior geometry.
papers.conclusion: Representation geometry is a practical blueprint for steering model behavior and offers insight into the inner workings of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering along the representation manifold produces output probabilities that follow the natural behavior manifold, while linear steering causes noisy, off-target effects.
The geometry of behavior and representation align bidirectionally, as paths in activation space based on representation and behavior manifolds are similar.
This alignment is observed across multiple concepts like days of the week, months, letters, ages, and in image-action models.
papers.abstract: What if the concept being manipulated in a neural network's representations isn't on a straight line, and how can steering along manifolds provide better control than linear steering? Shows that steering along manifolds in representation space provides better control of neural network behavior than linear steering, and reveals alignment between representation geometry and behavior geometry. Representation geometry is a practical blueprint for steering model behavior and offers insight into the inner workings of neural networks.

papers.title: Text-Trained LLMs Can Zero-Shot Extrapolate PDE Dynamics, Revealing a Three-Stage In-Context Learning Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can text-trained LLMs zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and what is the in-context learning mechanism behind this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a three-stage progression from syntax imitation to exploratory high-entropy phase to confident prediction.
papers.conclusion: Text-trained LLMs exhibit emergent zero-shot capability to extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a consistent three-stage progression, revealing inductive biases analogous to numerical methods.
papers.key_findings:
One-step prediction accuracy improves with longer temporal context but degrades with finer spatial discretization.
Multi-step rollouts show algebraic error growth with time horizon, similar to classical numerical solvers.
Token-level entropy analysis reveals a three-stage ICL progression: syntax imitation, exploratory high-entropy phase, and confident prediction.
LLMs can sustain coherent multi-step rollouts for nonlinear PDEs like Allen-Cahn and wave equations.
The three-stage progression is consistent across model sizes and PDE types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities across a range of tasks, including zero-shot time-series forecasting. We show that text-trained foundation models can accurately extrapolate spatiotemporal dynamics from discretized partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without fine-tuning or natural language prompting. Predictive accuracy improves with longer temporal contexts but degrades at finer spatial discretizations. In multi-step rollouts, where the model recursively predicts future spatial states over multiple time steps, errors grow algebraically with the time horizon, reminiscent of global error accumulation in classical finite-difference solvers. We interpret these trends as in-context neural scaling laws, where prediction quality varies predictably with both context length and output length. To better understand how LLMs are able to internally process PDE solutions so as to accurately roll them out, we analyze token-level output distributions and uncover a consistent three-stage ICL progression: beginning with syntactic pattern imitation, transitioning through an exploratory high-entropy phase, and culminating in confident, numerically grounded predictions.

papers.title: A PDE-based Explanation of Extreme Numerical Sensitivities and Edge of Stability in Training Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do extreme numerical sensitivities arise in training neural networks, and how are they linked to the Edge of Stability phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers restrained numerical instabilities in deep network training and provides a PDE-based theoretical framework explaining how they arise from exceeding stable learning rates, linking them to the Edge of Stability phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Numerical stability is a critical but previously overlooked factor in deep network training, and the PDE-based framework provides new insights into the Edge of Stability, suggesting the need for adaptive learning rate schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Floating-point arithmetic errors on the order of the smallest bit can be significantly amplified during training, leading to test accuracy variance comparable to that from SGD stochasticity.
Restrained instabilities occur when the learning rate exceeds the stability limit predicted by PDE analysis, causing localized oscillations without full divergence.
The Edge of Stability (EoS) is explained as a manifestation of these restrained instabilities in the training dynamics of CNNs.
The stability conditions depend on learning rate, weight decay, and network complexity, with larger networks more prone to such instabilities.
Both SGD and Adam optimizers exhibit restrained instabilities, indicating the phenomenon is fundamental to current training practices.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis focuses on deterministic gradient descent and a simplified CNN model, not fully accounting for stochasticity in SGD.
The analysis is primarily for convolutional neural networks; extension to other architectures (e.g., transformers) is not covered.
future_direction: Developing adaptive learning rate schemes that ensure stability while maintaining training speed.
Extending the analysis to stochastic gradient descent and other network architectures.
Investigating the role of regularization and network complexity in stability more thoroughly.
papers.abstract: We discover restrained numerical instabilities in current training practices of deep networks with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and its variants. We show numerical error (on the order of the smallest floating point bit and thus the most extreme or limiting numerical perturbations induced from floating point arithmetic in training deep nets can be amplified significantly and result in significant test accuracy variance (sensitivities), comparable to the test accuracy variance due to stochasticity in SGD. We show how this is likely traced to instabilities of the optimization dynamics that are restrained, i.e., localized over iterations and regions of the weight tensor space. We do this by presenting a theoretical framework using numerical analysis of partial differential equations (PDE), and analyzing the gradient descent PDE of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We show that it is stable only under certain conditions on the learning rate and weight decay. We show that rather than blowing up when the conditions are violated, the instability can be restrained. We show this is a consequence of the non-linear PDE associated with the gradient descent of the CNN, whose local linearization changes when over-driving the step size of the discretization, resulting in a stabilizing effect. We link restrained instabilities to the recently discovered Edge of Stability (EoS) phenomena, in which the stable step size predicted by classical theory is exceeded while continuing to optimize the loss and still converging. Because restrained instabilities occur at the EoS, our theory provides new insights and predictions about the EoS, in particular, the role of regularization and the dependence on the network complexity.

papers.title: Neural Networks Discover Physical Principles from Observation with an Intuitive World Model
papers.research_question: Can neural networks discover and explain physical principles (such as Newton's laws and Coulomb's law) from raw visual observations, similar to how humans learn intuitive physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Intuitive World Model (IWM), a neural network that learns physical principles (e.g., Newton's laws, Coulomb's law) from raw video data without built-in physics engines, and can provide explicit explanations and perform counterfactual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the Intuitive World Model (IWM) can learn physical principles from visual observation, providing explicit explanations and counterfactual reasoning, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
IWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on causal reasoning tasks (factual, predictive, counterfactual) on the ComPhy dataset.
IWM learns interpretable physical principles, as shown by its ability to generate force diagrams and explain physical events.
The hierarchical learning paradigm enables IWM to progressively learn appearance, velocity, mass, and charge representations.
IWM can perform counterfactual imagination by manipulating inferred physical properties (mass, charge) and generating plausible alternative scenarios.
The learned causal modules capture relationships analogous to Newton's laws and Coulomb's law, as demonstrated by sensitivity analysis.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Humans readily grasp physical principles via visual observation, underpinning our ability to model the world and reason about events. In contrast, AI systems often fail to extract consistent physical rules from video, relying on black-box mechanisms that produce implausible outcomes. We introduce the Intuitive World Model (IWM), designed to learn physical principles directly from vision, mimicking human intuition. Drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, IWM utilizes a modular architecture to decompose interactions into force-based dynamics. Through observing objects collide and interact via charges, it identifies intrinsic properties like mass and charge and learns representations analogous to Newton's and Coulomb's laws. This paradigm uniquely allows neural networks to provide explicit explanations for physical phenomena and conduct counterfactual reasoning consistent with learned physical laws. Our work demonstrates that a developmentally-inspired approach empowers AI to acquire explicit, interpretable physical knowledge from observation, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP.
