papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Deriving Decoder-Free Sparse Autoencoders from First Principles
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether implicit EM theory can be prescriptive, i.e., whether building a model exactly as the theory specifies yields a functioning system.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that implicit EM theory can be used to derive a working model (a decoder-free sparse autoencoder) that learns interpretable features and compares favorably to standard sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: Implicit EM theory is generative and can serve as a foundation for principled model design, as building exactly what the theory specifies yields a functioning model with confirmed predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The gradient of the LSE objective with respect to component distances equals the responsibility exactly, confirming the implicit EM identity.
Using only the LSE loss leads to complete collapse of components, as predicted by the theory.
Adding a variance penalty prevents dead components, and adding a decorrelation penalty prevents redundancy among components.
The learned features are interpretable digit prototypes, consistent with mixture components, unlike the unstructured features from a standard sparse autoencoder.
The derived model achieves higher linear probe accuracy (93.4%) and sparser representations with half the parameters compared to a standard sparse autoencoder baseline.
papers.limitation:
The model is a single linear layer with 64 components trained on MNIST; the theory's behavior at scale (deeper architectures, larger datasets) is untested.
The method is not tested on LLM activations, which are a primary motivation for sparse autoencoders.
The formal connection to EM is incomplete, lacking closed-form M-step updates and convergence guarantees.
Hyperparameters were not tuned systematically.
future_direction: Deriving closed-form M-steps for the linear case (explicit EM).
Applying InfoMax regularization during supervised learning to encourage mixture-like representations.

Using the framework for layer-wise pretraining, conditioning pretrained models, studying activation geometry, applying to attention, anomaly detection, optimal transport, and interpretability of existing models.
papers.abstract: Gradient descent on log-sum-exp (LSE) objectives performs implicit expectation--maximization (EM): the gradient with respect to each component output equals its responsibility. The same theory predicts collapse without volume control analogous to the log-determinant in Gaussian mixture models. We instantiate the theory in a single-layer encoder with an LSE objective and InfoMax regularization for volume control. Experiments confirm the theory's predictions. The gradient--responsibility identity holds exactly; LSE alone collapses; variance prevents dead components; decorrelation prevents redundancy. The model exhibits EM-like optimization dynamics in which lower loss does not correspond to better features and adaptive optimizers offer no advantage. The resulting decoder-free model learns interpretable mixture components, confirming that implicit EM theory can prescribe architectures.

papers.title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we extract interpretable control vectors from hidden states of motion transformers to modify motion forecasts at inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that motion transformers exhibit neural collapse towards interpretable features, allowing extraction of control vectors that can modify predictions at inference. Using sparse autoencoders improves the linearity of control vectors and enables zero-shot generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work advances mechanistic interpretability and controllability of motion transformers by showing neural collapse and extracting interpretable control vectors. Sparse dictionary learning improves linearity and enables zero-shot generalization.
papers.key_findings:
High linear probing accuracy indicates neural collapse toward interpretable motion features in hidden states of motion transformers.
Control vectors extracted from hidden states can modify motion forecasts at inference while preserving feasibility.
Sparse autoencoders optimize control vectors, leading to more linear changes in predictions when scaling control vectors.
The method enables zero-shot generalization to unseen dataset characteristics, such as domain shifts in driving style.
The approach has negligible computational overhead at inference.
papers.limitation:
Assumed a flat latent space and relied on vector arithmetic, leaving investigation of latent space curvature for future work.
Analysis limited to probing accuracy and class-distance normalized variance for measuring neural collapse.
future_direction: Investigate how SAE parameterization might address potential latent space curvature.
Explore safety validation in latent space for end-to-end driving.
Use control vectors to modify internal representations via instruction-based inputs.
Incorporate features from other modalities (static and dynamic scene elements).
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models generate hidden states that are difficult to interpret. In this work, we analyze hidden states and modify them at inference, with a focus on motion forecasting. We use linear probing to analyze whether interpretable features are embedded in hidden states. Our experiments reveal high probing accuracy, indicating latent space regularities with functionally important directions. Building on this, we use the directions between hidden states with opposing features to fit control vectors. At inference, we add our control vectors to hidden states and evaluate their impact on predictions. Remarkably, such modifications preserve the feasibility of predictions. We further refine our control vectors using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). This leads to more linear changes in predictions when scaling control vectors. Our approach enables mechanistic interpretation as well as zero-shot generalization to unseen dataset characteristics with negligible computational overhead.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Architecture through Continuous Dynamics: A Partial Differential Equation Perspective
papers.research_question: What is the mathematical necessity of core Transformer components (residual connections and layer normalization) when viewed through a continuous dynamics perspective? Can the Transformer's discrete layered structure be understood as a continuous spatiotemporal dynamical system governed by a PDE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a PDE-based framework that explains residual connections and layer normalization as mathematical stabilizers necessary for stable continuous dynamics in Transformers, showing that without them, the system suffers from representational drift and unstable training.
papers.conclusion: The Transformer's core components, often considered engineering heuristics, are in fact mathematical and dynamical stabilization mechanisms necessary to tame an otherwise unstable continuous system.
papers.key_findings:
The Transformer's layerwise evolution aligns with continuous PDE dynamics (depth-as-time hypothesis).
Residual connections prevent catastrophic representational drift by preserving input information across layers.
Layer normalization stabilizes training dynamics by preventing gradient explosion.
The Transformer exhibits a delayed compression strategy in information bottleneck terms, preserving intermediate representations for complex reasoning.
The PDE framework provides a first-principles explanation for the Transformer's design, showing that core components are necessary stabilizers.
papers.limitation: Reliance on mean-field approximation (ignoring batch-to-batch fluctuations), assumption of static parameters (disregarding training dynamics), and simplified treatment of multi-head attention.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture has revolutionized artificial intelligence, yet a principled theoretical understanding of its internal mechanisms remains elusive. This paper introduces a novel analytical framework that reconceptualizes the Transformer's discrete, layered structure as a continuous spatiotemporal dynamical system governed by a master Partial Differential Equation (PDE). Within this paradigm, we map core architectural components to distinct mathematical operators: self-attention as a non-local interaction, the feed-forward network as a local reaction, and, critically, residual connections and layer normalization as indispensable stabilization mechanisms. We do not propose a new model, but rather employ the PDE system as a theoretical probe to analyze the mathematical necessity of these components. By comparing a standard Transformer with a PDE simulator that lacks explicit stabilizers, our experiments provide compelling empirical evidence for our central thesis. We demonstrate that without residual connections, the system suffers from catastrophic representational drift, while the absence of layer normalization leads to unstable, explosive training dynamics. Our findings reveal that these seemingly heuristic "tricks" are, in fact, fundamental mathematical stabilizers required to tame an otherwise powerful but inherently unstable continuous system. This work offers a first-principles explanation for the Transformer's design and establishes a new paradigm for analyzing deep neural networks through the lens of continuous dynamics.

papers.title: The Evolving Nature of Latent Spaces: From GANs to Diffusion
papers.research_question: What is the nature of latent spaces in generative visual models, and how does the shift from GANs and VAEs to diffusion models challenge assumptions about unified internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that diffusion models fragment the burden of representation across layers, moving from 'synthesis in a strict sense' to 'synthesis in a broad sense', where unity emerges from distributed specialized processes.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models represent a shift from synthesis in a strict sense to synthesis in a broad sense, where coherence emerges from the distributed contributions of specialized layerwise representations.
papers.key_findings:
Diffusion models split the representational burden across layers, with different layers responsible for structure, content, and surface details.
The internal arrangements of representations differ across diffusion models, challenging the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Diffusion models lack a unified latent space with properties like density, smoothness, organization, and relevance as seen in GANs and VAEs.
The shift to diffusion models involves a specialization of labor in layerwise representations.
The concept of synthesis is redefined from strict to broad sense, emphasizing emergent configuration.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the evolving nature of internal representations in generative visual models, focusing on the conceptual and technical shift from GANs and VAEs to diffusion-based architectures. Drawing on Beatrice Fazi's account of synthesis as the amalgamation of distributed representations, we propose a distinction between "synthesis in a strict sense", where a compact latent space wholly determines the generative process, and "synthesis in a broad sense," which characterizes models whose representational labor is distributed across layers. Through close readings of model architectures and a targeted experimental setup that intervenes in layerwise representations, we show how diffusion models fragment the burden of representation and thereby challenge assumptions of unified internal space. By situating these findings within media theoretical frameworks and critically engaging with metaphors such as the latent space and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we argue for a reorientation of how generative AI is understood: not as a direct synthesis of content, but as an emergent configuration of specialized processes.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Improves Traversal of Hierarchical Knowledge in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reinforcement learning improve the traversal of hierarchical knowledge in LLMs, and how does it affect internal representations compared to base models?
papers.core_contribution: Reinforcement learning enhances LLMs' ability to traverse hierarchical knowledge structures by improving navigation skills rather than adding new knowledge, and structured prompting can mimic this improvement by guiding base models through systematic traversal.
papers.conclusion: RL enhances LLMs' hierarchical knowledge traversal by improving navigation mechanisms, suggesting efficient training paradigms that separate knowledge acquisition from organization.
papers.key_findings:
RL-enhanced models consistently outperform base and SFT models on pure knowledge recall tasks requiring hierarchical traversal.
Structured prompting reduces the performance gap between base and RL models, indicating that the necessary knowledge exists in base models but requires proper navigation.
RL models demonstrate superior path recall accuracy on deep-retrieval tasks with complex hierarchical navigation.
Layer-wise activation analysis shows that factual representations are similar between models, but query representations diverge, indicating RL transforms query processing.
Distilled models capture only surface-level improvements without acquiring robust navigation capabilities.
future_direction: Investigate these phenomena across broader domains
Develop RL mechanisms that explicitly optimize for hierarchical navigation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is often credited with improving language model reasoning and generalization at the expense of degrading memorized knowledge. We challenge this narrative by observing that RL-enhanced models consistently outperform their base and supervised fine-tuned (SFT) counterparts on pure knowledge recall tasks, particularly those requiring traversal of hierarchical, structured knowledge (e.g., medical codes). We hypothesize these gains stem not from newly acquired data, but from improved procedural skills in navigating and searching existing knowledge hierarchies within the model parameters. To support this hypothesis, we show that structured prompting, which explicitly guides SFTed models through hierarchical traversal, recovers most of the performance gap (reducing 24pp to 7pp on MedConceptsQA for DeepSeek-V3/R1). We further find that while prompting improves final-answer accuracy, RL-enhanced models retain superior ability to recall correct procedural paths on deep-retrieval tasks. Finally our layer-wise internal activation analysis reveals that while factual representations (e.g., activations for the statement "code 57.95 refers to urinary infection") maintain high cosine similarity between SFT and RL models, query representations (e.g., "what is code 57.95") diverge noticeably, indicating that RL primarily transforms how models traverse knowledge rather than the knowledge representation itself.

papers.title: Mask-Free Neuron Concept Annotation for Interpreting Neural Networks in Medical Domain
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in medical domains without requiring pixel-wise annotated datasets for neuron concept annotation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MAMMI, a mask-free neuron concept annotation method for medical image models that uses vision-language models and adaptive selection to handle class imbalance, outperforming previous methods.
papers.conclusion: MAMMI is an effective mask-free method for neuron concept annotation in medical vision models, addressing limitations of previous approaches and demonstrating superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
MAMMI achieves superior performance in neuron concept annotation compared to mask-based and other vision-language methods in medical settings.
Using a medical-specific concept set extracted from MIMIC-CXR reports significantly improves interpretability over general concept sets.
Adaptive neuron representative image selection effectively handles class-imbalanced data distributions and improves concept matching.
MedCLIP outperforms other CLIP models for medical concept annotation in MAMMI.
MAMMI accurately identifies neuron concepts at penultimate layers, whereas baselines like TSI and CLIP Dissect fail to do so.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in deep neural networks have shown promise in aiding disease diagnosis and medical decision-making. However, ensuring transparent decision-making processes of AI models in compliance with regulations requires a comprehensive understanding of the model's internal workings. However, previous methods heavily rely on expensive pixel-wise annotated datasets for interpreting the model, presenting a significant drawback in medical domains. In this paper, we propose a novel medical neuron concept annotation method, named Mask-free Medical Model Interpretation (MAMMI), addresses these challenges. By using a vision-language model, our method relaxes the need for pixel-level masks for neuron concept annotation. MAMMI achieves superior performance compared to other interpretation methods, demonstrating its efficacy in providing rich representations for neurons in medical image analysis. Our experiments on a model trained on NIH chest X-rays validate the effectiveness of MAMMI, showcasing its potential for transparent clinical decision-making in the medical domain. The code is available at https://github.com/ailab-kyunghee/MAMMI.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Transport Analysis of Infinitely Deep Neural Network
papers.research_question: Why do deep neural networks (DNNs) perform better than shallow models, and what do intermediate layers do?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the flow representation and transport analysis of DNNs, showing that deep denoising autoencoders (DAEs) transport mass to decrease the Shannon entropy of the data distribution, providing insights into the role of depth and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: The flow representation and transport analysis offer a novel framework for understanding DNNs, and further investigations may lead to interpretable and principled alternatives to DNNs.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper DAEs converge faster and extract better features than shallow DAEs.
Deep Gaussian DAE transports mass to decrease the Shannon entropy of the data distribution.
The stacked DAE is equivalent to the composition of DAEs, revealing the effect of pre-training as regularization of hidden layers.
The double continuum limit (integral representation of the flow representation) provides a new direction for mathematical modeling of DNNs.
The flow representation avoids the redundancy and complexity of ordinary DNN parametrization, enabling coordinate-free treatment.
future_direction: Further investigations on the double continuum limit to develop interpretable and principled alternatives to DNNs.
Development of interpretable and principled alternatives to DNNs based on the flow representation.
papers.abstract: We investigated the feature map inside deep neural networks (DNNs) by tracking the transport map. We are interested in the role of depth (why do DNNs perform better than shallow models?) and the interpretation of DNNs (what do intermediate layers do?) Despite the rapid development in their application, DNNs remain analytically unexplained because the hidden layers are nested and the parameters are not faithful. Inspired by the integral representation of shallow NNs, which is the continuum limit of the width, or the hidden unit number, we developed the flow representation and transport analysis of DNNs. The flow representation is the continuum limit of the depth or the hidden layer number, and it is specified by an ordinary differential equation with a vector field. We interpret an ordinary DNN as a transport map or a Euler broken line approximation of the flow. Technically speaking, a dynamical system is a natural model for the nested feature maps. In addition, it opens a new way to the coordinate-free treatment of DNNs by avoiding the redundant parametrization of DNNs. Following Wasserstein geometry, we analyze a flow in three aspects: dynamical system, continuity equation, and Wasserstein gradient flow. A key finding is that we specified a series of transport maps of the denoising autoencoder (DAE). Starting from the shallow DAE, this paper develops three topics: the transport map of the deep DAE, the equivalence between the stacked DAE and the composition of DAEs, and the development of the double continuum limit or the integral representation of the flow representation. As partial answers to the research questions, we found that deeper DAEs converge faster and the extracted features are better; in addition, a deep Gaussian DAE transports mass to decrease the Shannon entropy of the data distribution.

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: One-layer transformers fail to solve the induction heads task
papers.research_question: What are the size limitations of one-layer transformers in solving the induction heads task compared to two-layer transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that one-layer transformers cannot solve the induction heads task unless they are exponentially larger than two-layer transformers, using a communication complexity argument.
papers.conclusion: One-layer transformers are fundamentally limited in solving the induction heads task efficiently compared to two-layer transformers.
papers.key_findings: One-layer transformers require size hmp = Ω(n) to solve the induction heads task, which is exponentially larger than the size sufficient for two-layer transformers.
papers.abstract: A simple communication complexity argument proves that no one-layer transformer can solve the induction heads task unless its size is exponentially larger than the size sufficient for a two-layer transformer.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Robust Deep Interpretable Features for Binary Image Classification
papers.research_question: How can we find linearly separated latent representations? What implications on performance do such latent representations have? How can we interpret a model using linearly separated latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) framework, which combines deep generative models (IntroVAE) with a supervised objective based on kernel two-sample testing (ME objective) to encourage linear separation in the latent space, leading to more interpretable and robust features for binary image classification.
papers.conclusion: Combining deep generative modeling with a supervised kernel-based two-sample testing objective encourages separation between classes in the latent space, resulting in more interpretable features, improved classification performance with sparse linear models, and increased robustness to adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
DIF achieves better separation in the latent space compared to vanilla IntroVAE and a logistic separation objective, as visualized via UMAP.
DIF improves classification performance with sparser L1-regularized logistic regression models and in some cases outperforms CNN classifiers on test data.
Models trained with DIF exhibit improved robustness to adversarial attacks compared to vanilla models.
DIF isolates interpretable features that correspond to meaningful visual changes (e.g., facial hair, digit width, non-organ matter in lungs).
The imposed linear structure in the latent space leads to smooth latent traversals between classes without artifacts.
papers.limitation: The results presented for the COVID-19 x-ray data are for illustration purposes and further work is needed to draw any medically relevant conclusions based on them.
papers.abstract: The problem of interpretability for binary image classification is considered through the lens of kernel two-sample tests and generative modeling. A feature extraction framework coined Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) is developed, which is used in combination with IntroVAE, a generative model capable of high-resolution image synthesis. Experimental results on a variety of datasets, including COVID-19 chest x-rays demonstrate the benefits of combining deep generative models with the ideas from kernel-based hypothesis testing in moving towards more robust interpretable deep generative models.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: The Laplacian Mechanism Improves Transformers by Reshaping Token Geometry
papers.research_question: How does giving transformers more direct control over token variance (via the Laplacian mechanism) help them achieve an ideal token geometry and improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Laplacian mechanism, a simple modification to attention that gives transformers more direct control over token variance, leading to improved performance and the emergence of Neural Token Collapse—a geometry of maximal separability between classes.
papers.conclusion: The Laplacian mechanism improves transformers by allowing direct control over token variance, steering token representations toward Neural Token Collapse—a geometry with maximal class separability—and yielding consistent performance gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating Laplacian heads improves top-1 accuracy across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet classification tasks.
Laplacian heads reshape token embeddings toward a geometry of maximal separability, characterized by Neural Token Collapse (NTC).
The Laplacian mechanism shifts token variance from within-sequence to between-class, increasing between-class separability.
The Laplacian mechanism induces a steeper increase in cosine similarity between tokens within a sequence across transformer depth.
Laplacian heads promote a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF) structure in class means and classifier weights, as measured by Neural Collapse metrics.
papers.limitation: The investigation focused on supervised classification tasks; self-supervised learning objectives are fundamentally different and may require different optimal geometries.
future_direction: Characterize the optimal geometries for self-supervised learning tasks and study whether the Laplacian mechanism can steer token representations towards those ideals.
papers.abstract: Transformers leverage attention, the residual connection, and layer normalization to control the variance of token representations. We propose to modify attention into a Laplacian mechanism that gives the model more direct control over token variance. We conjecture that this helps transformers achieve the ideal token geometry. To investigate our conjecture, we first show that incorporating the Laplacian mechanism into transformers induces consistent improvements across benchmarks in computer vision and language. Next, we study how the Laplacian mechanism impacts the geometry of token representations using various tools: 1) principal component analysis, 2) cosine similarity metric, 3) analysis of variance, and 4) Neural Collapse metrics. Our investigation shows that the Laplacian mechanism reshapes token embeddings toward a geometry of maximal separability: tokens collapse according to their classes, and the class means exhibit Neural Collapse.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE) and finds that it underperforms standard SAEs due to excessive KL divergence regularization causing feature death, disproving the hypothesis that variational methods improve feature organization.
papers.conclusion: The naive application of variational methods to sparse autoencoders does not improve feature organization or interpretability and is not a promising direction for SAE development.
papers.key_findings:
The vSAE underperforms the standard TopK SAE across core metrics like CE loss, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
The vSAE exhibits catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to KL divergence pressure pushing activations toward zero.
The vSAE shows improved performance on Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR) and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) benchmarks, indicating more independent features.
t-SNE visualizations reveal that vSAE features are more dispersed and less clustered than SAE features, supporting the dispersive pressure hypothesis.
Despite having far fewer active features, the vSAE maintains feature interpretability, but the overall performance degradation suggests variational methods are not beneficial for SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The vSAE suffers from catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to excessive KL divergence regularization.
The observed improvements in feature independence (SCR, TPP) may be an artifact of the reduced dictionary size rather than principled organization.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting neural network representations by learning sparse, human-interpretable features from dense activations. We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability. We introduce the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE), which replaces deterministic ReLU gating with stochastic sampling from learned Gaussian posteriors and incorporates KL divergence regularization toward a standard normal prior. Our hypothesis is that this probabilistic sampling creates dispersive pressure, causing features to organize more coherently in the latent space while avoiding overlap. We evaluate a TopK vSAE against a standard TopK SAE on Pythia-70M transformer residual stream activations using comprehensive benchmarks including SAE Bench, individual feature interpretability analysis, and global latent space visualization through t-SNE. The vSAE underperforms standard SAE across core evaluation metrics, though excels at feature independence and ablation metrics. The KL divergence term creates excessive regularization pressure that substantially reduces the fraction of living features, leading to observed performance degradation. While vSAE features demonstrate improved robustness, they exhibit many more dead features than baseline. Our findings suggest that naive application of variational methods to SAEs does not improve feature organization or interpretability.

papers.title: Modeling the Influence of Data Structure on Learning in Neural Networks: The Hidden Manifold Model
papers.research_question: How does the structure of data (specifically, data lying on a lower-dimensional manifold) affect the learning dynamics and generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hidden Manifold Model (HMM), a generative model for structured data, and proves a Gaussian Equivalence Property (GEP) that enables analytical derivation of learning dynamics for two-layer neural networks trained with online stochastic gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Hidden Manifold Model provides a tractable framework for studying how data structure influences learning in neural networks, and the analytical results offer insights into the dynamics of specialization and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The Gaussian Equivalence Property holds for the HMM, allowing the learning dynamics to be described by a set of integro-differential equations.
Neural networks learn functions of increasing complexity during training, with a specialization transition where hidden units gradually align with teacher nodes.
Generalization performance deteriorates as the manifold dimension increases and improves with network width, but saturates beyond a certain width.
The learning rate has a minor influence on asymptotic error, but affects the time to reach specialization.
The HMM captures key properties of real data sets (MNIST, CIFAR10) in terms of learning dynamics and memorization patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding the reasons for the success of deep neural networks trained using stochastic gradientbased methods is a key open problem for the nascent theory of deep learning. The types of data where these networks are most successful, such as images or sequences of speech, are characterized by intricate correlations. Yet, most theoretical work on neural networks does not explicitly model training data or assumes that elements of each data sample are drawn independently from some factorized probability distribution. These approaches are, thus, by construction blind to the correlation structure of real-world datasets and their impact on learning in neural networks. Here, we introduce a generative model for structured datasets that we call the hidden manifold model. The idea is to construct high-dimensional inputs that lie on a lower-dimensional manifold, with labels that depend only on their position within this manifold, akin to a single-layer decoder or generator in a generative adversarial network. We demonstrate that learning of the hidden manifold model is amenable to an analytical treatment by proving a "Gaussian equivalence property" (GEP), and we use the GEP to show how the dynamics of two-layer neural networks trained using one-pass stochastic gradient descent is captured by a set of integro-differential equations that track the performance of the network at all times. This approach permits us to analyze in detail how a neural network learns functions of increasing complexity during training, how its performance depends on its size, and how it is impacted by parameters such as the learning rate or the dimension of the hidden manifold.

papers.title: From Black-Box to White-Box: Control-Theoretic Neural Network Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks mechanistically by treating them as nonlinear state-space systems and using control-theoretic tools like local linearization, controllability and observability Gramians, and Hankel singular values?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a control-theoretic framework that treats trained neural networks as nonlinear state-space systems and uses local linearization, controllability and observability Gramians, and Hankel singular values to analyze internal computation and identify important neurons and internal pathways.
papers.conclusion: The control-theoretic framework offers a simple, mathematically explicit lens for interpreting neural networks by identifying low-dimensional internal pathways and neuron importance, and can be extended to larger networks and transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The framework provides per-neuron controllability and observability energies, dominant internal modes, and a neuron-level importance metric.
Applied to a 1-2-2-1 SwiGLU network, the method identifies a dominant internal pathway and ranks neuron importance.
Applied to a 2-3-3-2 GELU network, the method shows that activation saturation reduces controllability, shrinks the dominant Hankel singular value, and shifts the dominant internal mode to a different subset of neurons.
papers.limitation: The framework is local and static: the analysis is performed around a fixed operating point and does not explicitly model temporal dynamics or training trajectories.
future_direction: Extending the approach to architectures with explicit dynamics to study how internal modes evolve along time or depth.
Applying the methodology to much larger and deeper networks using approximate techniques such as low-rank factorizations, randomized sketching, and layer-wise approximations.
Extending the framework to modern large language models (LLMs) and transformer architectures to identify controllable and influential directions in embedding space, neurons, or attention heads.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks achieve state of the art performance but remain difficult to interpret mechanistically. In this work, we propose a control theoretic framework that treats a trained neural network as a nonlinear state space system and uses local linearization, controllability and observability Gramians, and Hankel singular values to analyze its internal computation. For a given input, we linearize the network around the corresponding hidden activation pattern and construct a state space model whose state consists of hidden neuron activations. The input state and state output Jacobians define local controllability and observability Gramians, from which we compute Hankel singular values and associated modes. These quantities provide a principled notion of neuron and pathway importance: controllability measures how easily each neuron can be excited by input perturbations, observability measures how strongly each neuron influences the output, and Hankel singular values rank internal modes that carry input output energy. We illustrate the framework on simple feedforward networks, including a 1 2 2 1 SwiGLU network and a 2 3 3 2 GELU network. By comparing different operating points, we show how activation saturation reduces controllability, shrinks the dominant Hankel singular value, and shifts the dominant internal mode to a different subset of neurons. The proposed method turns a neural network into a collection of local white box dynamical models and suggests which internal directions are natural candidates for pruning or constraints to improve interpretability.

papers.title: Talking with the Latents -- how to convert your LLM into an astronomer
papers.research_question: How can domain-specific physical knowledge be introduced into Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable effective reasoning over complex numerical scientific data?
papers.core_contribution: A general framework for using LLMs as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces, enabling a single model to perform diverse tasks through natural language guidance by fusing pre-trained latent physical features with a pre-trained language model via a lightweight adapter and LoRA.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a domain-agnostic framework for aligning scientific foundation models with LLMs, marking a step toward developing scientifically capable and useful LLMs that can serve as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method enables effective reasoning over real scientific data, substantially outperforming strong baselines like Gemini 3 Pro without task-specific fine-tuning.
The model can combine latent information with general physical understanding to predict complex properties (e.g., stellar mass from radius).
The model can be 'steered' by identifying physically meaningful directions in the latent space, allowing for explicit physical manipulation and natural language interpretation.
Performance on complex tasks scales with LLM size, with larger models (Qwen-32B) performing best.
Sparse latent features are crucial for the LLM's successful interpretation, with models using sparse features outperforming those using dense features from a different encoder.
papers.limitation:
Relatively small LLMs and a simple unimodal spectra model were used.
The student model is fundamentally bounded by the quality and biases of the teacher's synthetic descriptions.
The architecture is unidirectional: it can describe data but cannot generate scientific data from text.
future_direction: To fully utilize the potential of this approach, larger LLMs and scientific foundation models should be used.
Enabling a bidirectional flow (generating scientific data from text) requires a different architecture and is a focus of future work.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer unique opportunities for scientific tasks, yet their ability to reason over complex numerical data remains largely unexplored. We propose a simple mechanism to introduce domain-specific physical knowledge into LLMs by fusing pre-trained latent physical features with a pre-trained language model. Our method employs a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework where a large LLM (teacher) generates synthetic question-answer supervision to transfer physical reasoning to a smaller LLM (student). The student is conditioned on latent physical features and trained via a lightweight adapter and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We demonstrate that this approach, applied to models with 1B, 8B, and 32B parameters, enables effective reasoning over real scientific data. Our models substantially outperform strong baselines, such as Gemini 3 Pro, across multiple downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. We show that the model combines latent information with general physical understanding to predict complex properties and can be "steered" by identifying physically meaningful directions in the latent space. This allows for explicit physical manipulation and natural language interpretation of latent structures. While our experiments focus on astrophysics, the framework is domain-agnostic and applicable to various scientific fields. Our main contribution is a general framework for using LLMs as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces, enabling a single model to perform diverse tasks through natural language guidance. This work marks a step toward developing scientifically capable and useful LLMs.

papers.title: How Transformers Get Rich: Approximation and Dynamics Analysis
papers.research_question: How do transformers implement induction heads, both in terms of approximation and learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis showing how two-layer transformers can approximate induction heads and characterizes the training dynamics with a sharp transition from n-gram to induction head learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently implement induction heads through specific roles of submodules, and learning induction heads involves a sharp transition from n-gram mechanisms driven by time-scale separation and component proportions.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer single-head transformers without FFNs can approximate vanilla induction heads.
Two-layer multi-head transformers without FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads (in-context n-gram).
Two-layer multi-head transformers with FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads with generic similarity functions.
Training dynamics on a mixed target show a sharp transition from 4-gram to induction head, with four phases.
The transition is driven by time-scale separation in self-attention and speed differences due to component proportions.
papers.limitation:
Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding may be nontrivial.
Dynamics analysis is limited to a simple mixed target without FFNs.
future_direction: Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding.
Generalizing dynamics analysis to nonlinear functions with FFNs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated exceptional in-context learning capabilities, yet the theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains limited. A recent work (Elhage et al., 2021) identified a ``rich'' in-context mechanism known as induction head, contrasting with ``lazy'' $n$-gram models that overlook long-range dependencies. In this work, we provide both approximation and dynamics analyses of how transformers implement induction heads. In the {\em approximation} analysis, we formalize both standard and generalized induction head mechanisms, and examine how transformers can efficiently implement them, with an emphasis on the distinct role of each transformer submodule. For the {\em dynamics} analysis, we study the training dynamics on a synthetic mixed target, composed of a 4-gram and an in-context 2-gram component. This controlled setting allows us to precisely characterize the entire training process and uncover an {\em abrupt transition} from lazy (4-gram) to rich (induction head) mechanisms as training progresses.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for PDE problems: a comprehensive review
papers.abstract: As AI for Science continues to grow, Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a transformative approach within the realm of scientific computing and deep learning, offering a robust and flexible framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) and other complex physical systems. By embedding physical laws directly into the architecture of neural networks, PINNs enable the integration of domain-specific knowledge, ensuring that the models adhere to known physics while fitting available data. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art advancements and applications of PINNs across a broad spectrum of PDE problems. In particular, focus is given on the PINN architectures, data resampling methods for PINN, loss and activation functions, feature embedding methods and so on. What’s more, the potential future directions and the anticipated evolution of PINNs are also discussed. We aim to provide valuable insights into PINNs for PDE problems, with hope to encourage further exploration and research in this promising area.

papers.title: Parameterized Physics-informed Neural Networks for Parameterized PDEs
papers.abstract: Complex physical systems are often described by partial differential equations (PDEs) that depend on parameters such as the Reynolds number in fluid mechanics. In applications such as design optimization or uncertainty quantification, solutions of those PDEs need to be evaluated at numerous points in the parameter space. While physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a new strong competitor as a surrogate, their usage in this scenario remains underexplored due to the inherent need for repetitive and time-consuming training. In this paper, we address this problem by proposing a novel extension, parameterized physics-informed neural networks (P$^2$INNs). P$^2$INNs enable modeling the solutions of parameterized PDEs via explicitly encoding a latent representation of PDE parameters. With the extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that P$^2$INNs outperform the baselines both in accuracy and parameter efficiency on benchmark 1D and 2D parameterized PDEs and are also effective in overcoming the known "failure modes".

papers.title: Learning PDE Solvers with Physics and Data: A Unifying View of Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are central to scientific modeling. Modern workflows increasingly rely on learning-based components to support model reuse, inference, and integration across large computational processes. Despite the emergence of various physics-aware data-driven approaches, the field still lacks a unified perspective to uncover their relationships, limitations, and appropriate roles in scientific workflows. To this end, we propose a unifying perspective to place two dominant paradigms: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Neural Operators (NOs), within a shared design space. We organize existing methods from three fundamental dimensions: what is learned, how physical structures are integrated into the learning process, and how the computational load is amortized across problem instances. In this way, many challenges can be best understood as consequences of these structural properties of learning PDEs. By analyzing advances through this unifying view, our survey aims to facilitate the development of reliable learning-based PDE solvers and catalyze a synthesis of physics and data.

papers.title: Enforcing Dirichlet boundary conditions in physics-informed neural networks and variational physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present and compare four methods to enforce Dirichlet boundary conditions in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks (VPINNs). Such conditions are usually imposed by adding penalization terms in the loss function and properly choosing the corresponding scaling coefficients; however, in practice, this requires an expensive tuning phase. We show through several numerical tests that modifying the output of the neural network to exactly match the prescribed values leads to more efficient and accurate solvers. The best results are achieved by exactly enforcing the Dirichlet boundary conditions by means of an approximate distance function.
